verdict: E-Q27 VERDICT (does the ternary zero do work? — binary vs ternary vs 4-level on both sealed arms, arm-filtered live queries, strict scoring): H1 LIVES — C22 LIVES — DECISIVELY, on BOTH arms: ternary beats binary by 0.25 on the score arm (0.60 vs 0.35) and 0.2 on the noul arm (0.60 vs 0.40): the sign alone loses five records per arm; the middle level carries real information (the zero says 'this record is TYPICAL here' — a refusal the binary code cannot express). H2 LIVES via the diminishing-returns clause: the ternary-to-4-level gain (-0.05 on S, 0.1 on N) is smaller than the binary-to-ternary gain on both arms — but the arms DIVERGE at the 4th level: the score arm SATURATES at ternary (SQ 0.55 < ST 0.6 — the ordinal spread's information is exhausted by 3 levels) while the noul arm KEEPS CLIMBING (NQ 0.7 — the calibrated mass buys two more records from the 4th level). H3 DIES: the T-B gap is SMALLER on the noul arm (0.2 vs 0.25) — the saturation-interaction prediction inverted; the zero-mass receipt explains it: ST 0.25 vs NT 0.2375 — the noul arm does NOT have more zeros (P3 MISS; both arms sit near 0.24, below the predicted ranges). THE QUANTIZATION CURVES: S: 0.35 -> 0.6 -> 0.55 -> 0.70 (continuous); N: 0.4 -> 0.6 -> 0.7 -> 0.80. THE CONSUMER LAW: the marginal value of quantization levels is ARM-DEPENDENT — ordinal spread saturates at 3 levels; calibrated mass keeps paying to 4. At equal PRACTICAL storage (2 bits/axis packed) the 4-level noul code (0.70) is the best 16-bit configuration; the ternary code remains the algebra-capable one (the E-Q26 offset arithmetic operates on {-1,0,+1} codes) and the theory-efficient one (~1.5 bits/axis measured). Binary is never the right choice on this corpus: the zero is worth five records.
